Issued at 133 AM MDT Thu Oct 8 2026

It certainly has been a very warm start to October, and this has 
been the theme for much of the year. Through the first seven days of 
the month, all of our major climate sites are ranked in at least the 
top 5 of all time warmest first seven days of October, with several 
ranking as the warmest. And we will have at least two more days of 
warm temperatures, with some locations having three more. However, 
we will get a slap across the face into reality as we have a greater 
than 9 in 10 chance of seeing much cooler temperatures, numerous 
rain showers and, for the higher elevations, the first good snow of 
the season.

We have no real issues today as ridging will continue to control the 
weather across the area today. All in all, it looks like another 
nice day, although feeling more like early September than early 
October with temperatures well above normal once again. Highs should 
be fairly close to what was seen yesterday. So if you can, get out 
and enjoy it. 

The first signs of change will move in tomorrow. Not with 
temperatures, as highs will likely be a few degrees warmer than on 
Thursday. However, a cold front will be dropping out of Canada, the 
strongest front of the year. With the ridge beginning to flatten and 
the pressure gradient tightening, a gusty wind will develop across 
portions of the area. This will especially be the case in areas 
favored by southwest flow, especially from Rock Springs into 
southern Johnson County. The area with the current fire weather 
watch looks reasonable given the this is where the strongest wind 
will be and the mean lowest relative humidity is below 15 percent. 
The one additional area I considered was the Cody Foothills, but 
humidity may not be low enough. We will let the day shift take 
another look. We will continue the Fire Weather Watch as is for now 
as a result. There is a very small chance for a shower or 
thunderstorm in Sweetwater County with a bit of mid level moisture 
creeping northward, but the chance is less than 1 out of 6 for all 
locations.

The change really begins on Saturday. The aforementioned cold front 
approaches the state. At the same time, we will begin to see some 
moisture from Rachel, and I don't Jennifer Aniston's character from 
the 90s sitcom "Friends" that popularized the haircut of the same 
name. Moisture will be drawn northward between the ridge to the 
south and an upper level low over the Pacific northwest and channeled 
into the intermountain west. The main action here will be in western 
Wyoming, moving East of the Divide later in the day. At least during 
the day, any precipitation would fall as rain. This will bring 
another above normal temperature day across areas East of the 
Divide, although cooler than on Friday. Most guidance has also 
slowed the progress of the front a bit. Both the GFS and the 
European have the 700 millibar celsius line near the Montana-Wyoming 
Border by 12Z Sunday. As a result, snow levels should remain above 
pass level with the possible exception of Beartooth Pass.

At this point, the heaviest and steadiest precipitation looks to be 
on Sunday into Sunday night. The remnants of Rachel should be 
scooped up by and upper level low over California and moved rapidly 
northward. With the southwest flow, the heaviest precipitation would 
again fall in western Wyoming with the upslope flow, especially in 
places like the Wind River Range, the Tetons and the Absarokas. All 
areas will have a good chance of rain though. The NBM ensemble gives 
a greater than 1 out of 2 chance of a quarter of an inch of 
precipitation over the entire area, with a near 100 percent chance in 
western Wyoming. Much of western Wyoming, especially the mountains, 
has a greater than a 1 in 2 chance of an inch or more of QPF from 
Sunday through Sunday night. Precipitable water values are anomalously 
high at this time, topping out at around 0.85 inches, which is 
greater than 150 percent of normal. We do have a marginal risk of 
excessive rainfall over the area as well. One thing that may 
mitigate this threat is that with the cooler temperatures, it may be 
more stratiform than convective but we have to watch it. 

The next question a lot of people are asking is, what about snow? 
Here is where there is a bit more uncertainty, at least for the 
lower elevations. We continue to have some differences in how cold 
it will get. There is as much as a 3 to 4 degree difference in the 
crucial 700 millibar temperatures. For example, the GFS keeps it 
warmer, which would hold snow levels at 8500 feet or higher. The 
European drops the temperature to minus 4, which lowers snow levels 
down to 6000 to 6500 feet across northern Wyoming. This implications 
for a place like Cody, where if precipitation is heavy enough it 
could bring enough evaporative cooling to change rain to snow. The
